title: Episode 3: Navigating Repositories
description: Exploring a repository: tabs, files, README, branches, and commit history.
concepts: What a repository is: a project folder tracked by Git
The repository tab bar: Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, Settings
The Code tab: file tree, README rendering, branch selector
What a branch is and why repositories have them
The default branch (usually main) and what it means
Reading commit history: who changed what and when
What cloning means: copying a remote repo to your computer
The difference between cloning and forking
Using gh repo clone versus git clone versus downloading a ZIP
The About section, topics, and license on a repository page
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're getting comfortable inside GitHub repositories: how they're laid out, how to orient yourself quickly with a screen reader or keyboard, and how to move from, "I found a repo," to, "I actually know where things are."

[JAMIE]
And this is one of those chapters where the goal is not speed, right? It's confidence.

[ALEX]
Exactly. This is a foundation lesson. There are no challenge tasks here, no automation checks. The point is to build a reliable mental map before later chapters ask you to work with issues, pull requests, and traceable contributions.

[JAMIE]
So if someone's feeling pressure to perform already, this is a good place to exhale.

[ALEX]
Yes. Think of this as orientation practice. Learn the page structure, practice basic movement keys like heading navigation and landmark navigation, confirm you feel ready with a peer or facilitator if you have one, and then move on. It's a safety-first learning pattern.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we dive in, what companion resources matter here?

[ALEX]
A few. There's an episode version of this lesson for preview or review. There's a glossary appendix and a screen reader cheat sheet appendix. And there are two especially useful outside references: GitHub Docs on repositories, and GitHub's own accessibility guide for using repositories with a screen reader.

[JAMIE]
And that official accessibility guide is NVDA-focused, right?

[ALEX]
Right. This lesson covers the same general territory but adds workshop guidance, VoiceOver perspectives, low-vision workflows, and some command-line connection points.

[JAMIE]
I also noticed the chapter talks about learning cards.

[ALEX]
Yes. Throughout the written material, there are expandable learning cards. Not every card appears at every step. They're there so people can open the guidance that fits how they work. The four types are: visual and mouse guidance, low vision guidance for zoom or high contrast users, screen reader guidance for NVDA or JAWS on Windows, and screen reader guidance for VoiceOver on macOS.

[JAMIE]
So the lesson is shared, but the access path can differ.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's start with the basic question: what is a repository page?

[JAMIE]
Because people hear "repo" all the time, but the page itself has a structure.

[ALEX]
It does. When you visit a URL like github dot com slash owner slash repo-name, you usually land on the repository home page, which is also the Code tab. That page has several dependable parts even if the visual arrangement shifts.

[JAMIE]
That "even if" seems important for accessibility.

[ALEX]
Very important. GitHub can change visual placement depending on screen width, account features, repository settings, and ongoing product changes. So instead of memorizing a fixed visual layout, it's better to rely on stable structural cues: the global navigation, the repository's main heading, the repository navigation landmark, the Code tab, the branch selector, the file list, an optional About sidebar, and often a rendered README.

[JAMIE]
So the visual order might look familiar on a wide desktop screen, but learners shouldn't treat that as a promise.

[ALEX]
Exactly. On a big screen you might often perceive: global nav, repo header, tab row, file and code panel, optional sidebar, then README content. But for accessible navigation, use headings, landmarks, tab names, and shortcuts to re-orient instead of trusting a visual map alone.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay. I open a repository for the first time. What should I expect to hear or find first?

[ALEX]
Three big things. First, the page title is often announced in a format like owner slash repo-name, then a short description, then GitHub. Second, if you press the number 1 key to jump to the first level-one heading, you should land on the repo name. Third, the tab bar lives in a landmark labeled Repository navigation.

[JAMIE]
And there's an orientation routine the chapter wants people to repeat on every new repo.

[ALEX]
Yes, and it's worth making habitual. Step one: press 1 and hear the repository name. Step two: press D to move through landmarks and learn the page structure. Step three: open your headings list"”NVDA plus F7, or VoiceOver plus U and then look at headings"”to understand what sections exist on this page.

[JAMIE]
That sounds simple, but it's really a way to reduce that "where am I?" feeling.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And as you move through landmarks with D, some key names often appear. Repository Navigation is the tab bar. Main contains the file tree, branch selector, repo details, and contributors. Repository Files Navigation often contains the rendered README content. Within each landmark, headings"”often level 2"”help break things into chunks.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk about the tabs. Those are easy to overlook if you're overwhelmed.

[ALEX]
Right. Repository tabs are a major control surface. Common tabs include Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Discussions, Actions, Projects, Wiki, Security, Insights, and Settings. But not every repository shows all of them. Discussions, Wiki, and Projects have to be enabled, and Settings is usually only visible to maintainers.

[JAMIE]
How do people reach them accessibly?

[ALEX]
For screen reader users on Windows, press D to jump to the Repository navigation landmark, then use K for links or Tab to move between tab links. For VoiceOver, use the rotor to jump to landmarks, find Repository navigation, then move through items within it.

[JAMIE]
And for low-vision users?

[ALEX]
At higher zoom levels, the tabs may wrap onto two lines, but they remain standard links. The active tab is typically shown with an underline. In Windows High Contrast mode, that underline uses the system accent color. If it's hard to click precisely at high zoom, Tab through the links instead.

[JAMIE]
The chapter also mentions shortcuts to jump straight to some tabs.

[ALEX]
Yes. GitHub supports some two-key shortcuts. G then I jumps to Issues. G then P jumps to Pull Requests. Those are handy when you already know where you want to go.

[JAMIE]
And what do tab labels sound like with a screen reader?

[ALEX]
Usually the tab name plus a count. For example, "Issues, 14 open," or "Pull requests, 3 open." If the tab is the one you're currently on, the screen reader may announce it as selected or current.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now we're on the Code tab. What's the centerpiece there?

[ALEX]
The files table. This is the heart of the repository home page. It lists the folders and files in the current location.

[JAMIE]
How do you reach it?

[ALEX]
For screen reader users, one fast method is pressing T to jump to the next table on the page. The first table is often the files table, and you may hear something like, "table with N rows and 3 columns."

[JAMIE]
And visually?

[ALEX]
It's usually just below the branch selector in the main content area. It generally has three columns: Name, Message, and Age or Date. Name is the file or folder name. Message is the most recent commit message affecting that item. Age is how long ago that change happened.

[JAMIE]
That's more informative than just a file listing.

[ALEX]
Yes. It tells you not only what exists, but also recent activity. That helps you identify active areas of a project.

[JAMIE]
What about people using magnification?

[ALEX]
At 200 percent zoom or more, the message and date columns may truncate. Tooltips may reveal full text on hover. The icons for folders and files remain visible, and in high contrast they should use system colors with visible outlines. The chapter also suggests using browser Find, Control plus F, to locate a visible file name on the page, and using Go to file for faster searching.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Once I'm in the table, how do I actually read it well with a screen reader?

[ALEX]
Think row by row. Move to the Name column first, hear the file or folder name, move right to hear the latest commit message, and right again to hear the age. So a row might effectively read as, "docs slash, Add accessibility guide, 3 days ago."

[JAMIE]
And there are table navigation keys depending on the screen reader.

[ALEX]
Yes. For NVDA and JAWS, people often use Control Alt with the arrow keys to move among cells. For VoiceOver, VO Shift with arrow keys is common in tables. To open a file or folder, activate the link in the Name column"”Enter on Windows, or VO Space on Mac.

[JAMIE]
How do you tell folders from files?

[ALEX]
Folders end with a slash in the Name column. Opening a folder reloads the page to show that folder's contents. To move back up, use the browser Back button or the breadcrumb links if present.

[JAMIE]
So one little slash matters a lot.

[ALEX]
It really does.

[JAMIE]
And the learning-card spirit here is basically: jump to the table, confirm columns, read rows in order, and activate only from the name cell.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That pattern keeps you oriented.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Next up: branches. People hear "branch" early in Git, but on the repository page there's a specific control for it.

[ALEX]
Right, the branch selector. It lets you switch which branch"”or sometimes tag"”you're viewing.

[JAMIE]
How do you open it?

[ALEX]
Usually there's a button near the top of the file listing area labeled something like the current branch name, often main. Activating it opens a dropdown or dialog for switching branches and tags.

[JAMIE]
What's inside that dropdown?

[ALEX]
Typically a search field and lists for branches and tags. You can type to filter results. This is useful in repositories with many branches.

[JAMIE]
And tags matter because they often represent releases.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Switching to a tag lets you view the repository as it existed at a specific labeled point, often a release version. That's very useful when you want to inspect what was in a release without following ongoing work on the main branch.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's connect that to cloning, because people often confuse "I can view it in the browser" with "I have it on my computer."

[ALEX]
Yes. Cloning means making a local copy of the repository on your machine so you can inspect or work with it using Git and your editor.

[JAMIE]
The chapter has a nice practical angle here: you don't always need the full URL.

[ALEX]
Right. With GitHub CLI, you can often clone using the repository owner and name directly"”something like gh repo clone owner slash repo-name"”without manually copying a URL. And a common pattern is to clone and then immediately change into the new folder.

[JAMIE]
What if you're using standard Git instead of GitHub CLI?

[ALEX]
Then you'd use git clone with an HTTPS or SSH URL, depending on your setup. The concept is the same: Git downloads the repository history and working files into a local directory.

[JAMIE]
What are the main teaching points from the cloning learning cards and tool cards?

[ALEX]
First, know what tool you're using: browser only, GitHub CLI, or standard Git. Second, understand that cloning is local; it does not create a separate GitHub copy. Third, after cloning, you typically cd into the folder so your terminal context matches the repository. And fourth, if you want to contribute but don't have write access, cloning alone may not be enough"”you may also need a fork.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Perfect transition: fork versus clone versus branch.

[ALEX]
This distinction is foundational. A clone is a local copy on your own computer. A fork is a copy of someone else's repository under your own GitHub account. A branch is a parallel line of work inside one repository.

[JAMIE]
So if I say, "I made a branch," I did not make a new repository.

[ALEX]
Correct. And if you say, "I cloned the repo," you probably still mean the same repository, just locally on disk. If you say, "I forked it," you now have your own GitHub-hosted copy.

[JAMIE]
When does each one matter?

[ALEX]
Clone when you want local access. Fork when you need your own remote copy, especially for contributing to a project where you don't have direct write permissions. Branch when you want to isolate a feature, fix, or experiment within a repository.

[JAMIE]
That clears up a lot.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The repository page also has those social or workflow buttons: watch, star, fork.

[ALEX]
Yes, and they do different jobs. Watching subscribes you to notifications. Starring bookmarks the repository for later and signals interest. Forking creates your own copy under your account.

[JAMIE]
So starring is not subscribing.

[ALEX]
Right. If you star a project, you're saying, "I want to remember this." If you watch it, you're saying, "Tell me what's happening here." If you fork it, you're saying, "I want my own copy to work from."

[JAMIE]
That's a really useful three-part distinction.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now suppose I activate a file from the files table. What does a single file page look like?

[ALEX]
A file page has its own landmarks and structure. You'll encounter the file path, file content, and action buttons for operations like raw view, blame, history, edit, download, or copy link, depending on permissions and file type.

[JAMIE]
Let's break that into markdown files versus code files.

[ALEX]
Good idea. If you open a Markdown file like README dot md, GitHub often shows a rendered reading view. That means headings, lists, links, and code blocks are presented in a more readable document format.

[JAMIE]
Which can be much easier to navigate with heading commands.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A rendered README often behaves like a structured document inside the repository page. You can use heading navigation, links lists, and other document-reading strategies.

[JAMIE]
What about code files?

[ALEX]
Code files are typically shown line by line, often with line numbers. The reading experience is denser. Depending on your screen reader and mode, you may move through lines, review syntax-heavy text, and use the file controls to switch to raw view or blame if that helps.

[JAMIE]
And those action buttons"”how do people reach them?

[ALEX]
Usually by navigating near the file header area, around the file title and controls. With a screen reader, landmark and heading navigation can get you close, then Tab or link/button navigation can reach the specific actions.

[JAMIE]
What kinds of actions should learners expect?

[ALEX]
Common ones include viewing raw file contents, opening blame, viewing history, editing the file if you have permission or are working in your fork, and sometimes downloading. The exact set can vary.

[JAMIE]
Editing from the browser sounds convenient, but also potentially risky if you're still learning.

[ALEX]
That's why the chapter's tone is careful. Browser editing exists, and it can be useful for small changes, especially in your own fork or for minor documentation fixes. But learners should stay oriented: know which branch they're on, know whether they're editing upstream or their own fork, and understand that saving in the browser creates a commit path.

[JAMIE]
So the learning card message is: read the file structure first, then use action buttons intentionally.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's also the blame view, which has a dramatic name.

[ALEX]
It does, but it's very practical. Blame shows each line of a file annotated with the commit and author who last changed that line.

[JAMIE]
So if I want to know who touched a section recently, blame is the tool.

[ALEX]
Yes. It connects lines of code or text back to specific commits. That can help you understand why a change happened, who made it, and whether a pattern in the file is recent or old.

[JAMIE]
How do you navigate it?

[ALEX]
Carefully and in chunks. The page often pairs commit metadata with file lines. Screen reader users may need to move between links, line annotations, and code content, so headings, landmarks, and structured navigation become extra important. It's less about speed and more about tracing context.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Then we have commit history.

[ALEX]
Yes. A repository or file can expose commit history, and it's one of the best ways to understand project activity over time.

[JAMIE]
What does the commits list page usually contain?

[ALEX]
A list of commits, often with commit messages, authors, dates, and links to individual commit pages. Reading the list gives you a sense of project rhythm: frequent changes, documentation work, bug fixes, release preparation, and so on.

[JAMIE]
And an individual commit page?

[ALEX]
That page usually includes the commit message, metadata like author and time, the commit identifier, parent relationships, and a diff showing what changed. The diff is where you inspect additions and deletions.

[JAMIE]
So the commits list tells you what happened broadly, and the commit page tells you exactly what changed.

[ALEX]
Well said.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Searching for a file is another huge practical skill, especially in large repositories.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. The fastest browser-based method is often Go to file.

[JAMIE]
How does that work?

[ALEX]
GitHub supports a keyboard shortcut"”T on many repository pages"”to open a file finder. You start typing part of a file name or path, the list filters as you type, and then you select the result you want.

[JAMIE]
That beats arrowing through dozens or hundreds of rows in a files table.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It's especially helpful at high magnification, for screen reader users who want to reduce navigation load, and for anyone working in a big codebase. The learning-card takeaway is simple: if you know even part of the file name, use Go to file.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The chapter also calls out GitHub shortcuts in a kind of spotlight section.

[ALEX]
Yes. Shortcuts can save a lot of effort once you're already oriented. We already mentioned G then I for Issues, G then P for Pull Requests, and T for Go to file. The broader lesson is not to memorize everything at once, but to adopt a few that reduce friction.

[JAMIE]
There's also mention of navigating the sidebar.

[ALEX]
Right. Some repository pages include a sidebar with About information, links, releases, packages, contributor summaries, or related metadata. Depending on viewport and page design, it may appear before or after the main content in reading order. Again, don't rely on sighted layout assumptions"”use headings and landmarks to find it.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's focus on that About section for a moment. Why does it matter?

[ALEX]
Because it often answers the first practical questions: What does this project do? Where is its homepage? What topics or tags describe it? Does it have releases or package information? The About section is quick orientation metadata.

[JAMIE]
So if I'm evaluating whether a repo is even relevant to me, About is part of the answer.

[ALEX]
Yes, along with the description and README.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I love the practical scenarios section because it translates features into real intentions. Can we walk through those?

[ALEX]
Definitely.

[JAMIE]
Scenario A: "I want to find out what this project does."

[ALEX]
Start with the repository name and short description. Then find the About section if present. Then read the README, especially its opening paragraphs and headings. If the README is rendered, heading navigation is your friend. This sequence usually gives you purpose, scope, installation hints, and whether the project is active.

[JAMIE]
Scenario B: "I want to find a good file to edit."

[ALEX]
Begin on the files table. Look for documentation files like README, CONTRIBUTING, docs folders, or clearly named small files. Read the Message and Age columns to see which areas are active. Use Go to file if you know the likely target. And if the project has contribution guidance, read that before editing.

[JAMIE]
Scenario C: "I want to know who has been working on this file recently."

[ALEX]
Open the file, then use History or Blame. History shows commits affecting the file over time. Blame shows who last changed each line. Together, they help you identify recent contributors and active sections.

[JAMIE]
Scenario D: "I want to understand what changed in the last release."

[ALEX]
Use the branch or tag selector to switch to a release tag if needed, look for Releases information, and read recent commit history or release notes. If the repository uses tags consistently, comparing current code to a tagged version can clarify what changed around that release.

[JAMIE]
Scenario E: "I want to contribute"”where do I start?"

[ALEX]
First, understand the project: description, About, README. Next, check whether there's a CONTRIBUTING file, issue templates, or discussions about newcomer tasks. Then decide your workflow: if you lack write access, you may need to fork; in any case, you'll likely clone locally and work on a branch. And watch for repository norms in issues and pull requests.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What if someone gets stuck while navigating?

[ALEX]
Return to basics. Press 1 to confirm the repository heading. Use D to cycle through landmarks. Open the headings list. If you're lost in a long page, go back to known structural anchors instead of pushing forward blindly. You can also reload the page, return to the Code tab, or use a direct shortcut like G then I if your goal has changed.

[JAMIE]
So getting unstuck is really a re-orientation skill.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Not a failure"”just a normal part of accessible navigation.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The chapter ends with a try-it activity: the five-tab tour. What's the spirit of that exercise?

[ALEX]
To make navigation concrete. Visit a repository and intentionally tour several tabs"”typically Code, Issues, Pull Requests, maybe Actions or Wiki if available, and then back again. The purpose is to feel how the tab bar behaves, how the page structure shifts, and how you can keep re-orienting with headings, landmarks, and shortcuts.

[JAMIE]
So not "memorize every control," but "practice moving with confidence."

[ALEX]
Yes. Learn the terrain by traversing it.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, can you summarize the most important mental model from this lesson?

[ALEX]
A repository page is not just a wall of links. It's a structured workspace with repeatable landmarks: heading, repository navigation, code and files area, optional sidebar, and file or README content. If you learn to orient with headings, landmarks, tabs, tables, and a few shortcuts, GitHub becomes much more predictable.

[JAMIE]
And the big workflow vocabulary?

[ALEX]
Clone is local. Fork is your own remote copy. Branch is an isolated line of work within a repository. Watch subscribes. Star bookmarks. Blame traces lines to commits. History traces files and repositories over time. Go to file helps you jump directly where you need to go.

[JAMIE]
That's a strong toolkit.

[ALEX]
It is. And it's enough to make the next chapters much less intimidating.

[JAMIE]
Thanks everyone. Take a little time to practice the orientation sequence on a real repository: first heading, landmarks, headings list, tabs, files table, and one file page. That repetition pays off.

[ALEX]
And if you need authoritative backup, GitHub Docs and GitHub's accessibility guide are excellent companions. We'll continue building from here.

# Navigating Repositories
>
> **Listen to Episode 3:** [Navigating Repositories](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix A: Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md) | [Appendix B: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/about-repositories) | [GitHub Accessibility Guide: Repositories](https://accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/repos/)

## A Screen Reader Guide to GitHub Repositories

> This guide covers everything you need to explore a GitHub repository using your keyboard and screen reader. No mouse required.

> **Official GitHub Accessibility Guide:** GitHub publishes an NVDA-focused guide for navigating repositories with a screen reader at [Using GitHub Repositories with a Screen Reader](https://accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/repos/). This chapter covers the same material with additional perspectives (VoiceOver, low vision, CLI) and workshop-specific guidance. Use the official guide as a companion reference.

## Workshop Recommendation (Chapter 3)

Chapter 3 is a **confidence-building orientation chapter**.

- **Challenge count:** none
- **Automation check:** none
- **Why:** this chapter teaches navigation foundations that are practiced in later issue and PR chapters.

### Safety-First Learning Pattern

Use this sequence before moving to graded chapters:

1. Learn the page structure (heading, landmarks, tabs).
2. Practice orientation (`1`, `D`, heading list).
3. Confirm readiness with a peer or facilitator.
4. Move to Chapter 4 for Learning Room orientation, then Chapter 5 for issue-based, traceable challenges.

### About Learning Cards in This Chapter

This chapter provides learning cards: expandable blocks that offer perspective-specific guidance for different ways of working. Not every card appears at every step. Open the ones that match how you work.

The following table describes the four learning card types used in this chapter.

| Card | Who it helps | What it covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visual / mouse | Sighted users navigating with a mouse or trackpad | Click targets, visual cues, layout orientation |
| Low vision | Users with magnification, zoom, or high-contrast themes | Zoom-friendly navigation, locating controls at high magnification |
| Screen reader (NVDA / JAWS) | Screen reader users on Windows | Keystroke sequences, Focus and Browse mode, landmark navigation |
| Screen reader (VoiceOver) | Screen reader users on macOS | VO key sequences, rotor usage, interaction model |

## What Is a Repository Page?

When you navigate to a GitHub repository (e.g., `https://github.com/owner/repo-name`), you land on the **repository home page** (also called the Code tab). This page has several distinct regions:

### Description

GitHub can change visual placement based on viewport width, account features, repository settings, and product rollout. The dependable structure is the set of named regions and controls: the global navigation, the repository H1 heading, the **Repository navigation** landmark, the **Code** tab, the branch selector, the file list, optional repository sidebar information, and the rendered `README.md` when present.

On a wide desktop layout, these often appear in a familiar order: global navigation, repository header, repository tabs, file/code panel, optional sidebar, and rendered README. Teach that order as a map, not as a guarantee. When the visual order differs, use headings, landmarks, tab names, and keyboard shortcuts to re-orient.

## Landing on a Repository - What to Expect

When you first navigate to a repo URL:

1. **The page title** is announced with the format: `owner/repo-name: Short description - GitHub`
2. **First heading** (`1` key) will navigate to the repo name: "owner/repo-name"
3. **The tab bar** is a landmark labeled "Repository navigation"

### Orientation sequence (do this on every new repo)

```text
Step 1: Press 1 - hear the repo name
Step 2: Press D - navigate through landmarks to learn page structure
Step 3: Press NVDA+F7 (or VO+U) - scan headings to understand what's on the page
```

> **Key landmark names you will hear with `D`:** Repository pages have three main landmark sections: **"Repository Navigation"** (the tab bar), **"Main"** (the file tree, branch selector, repo details, and contributors), and **"Repository Files Navigation"** (the rendered README content). Within each landmark, press `H` or `2` to navigate subsections - most are organized under heading level 2.

## Navigating the Repository Tabs

The main tabs are: **Code**, **Issues**, **Pull Requests**, **Discussions**, **Actions**, **Projects**, **Wiki**, **Security**, **Insights**, and **Settings** (Settings only visible to maintainers). Not all tabs appear on every repository - Discussions, Wiki, and Projects must be enabled by the repository owner.

### How to reach the tabs

<details>
<summary>Visual / mouse users</summary>

The tab bar is visible just below the repository name. Click the tab you want - **Code**, **Issues**, **Pull requests**, etc. The active tab is underlined. The number next to a tab (e.g., "Issues · 14") shows how many open items are in that section.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users (zoom, high contrast)</summary>

The tab bar is just below the repository name. At 200% browser zoom or higher:

- The tabs may wrap to two lines. Each tab remains a standard link.
- The active tab is indicated by an underline. In Windows High Contrast mode, the underline uses the system accent color.
- Tab counts ("Issues · 14") appear as part of each tab's text and remain readable at high magnification.
- If tabs are hard to click at high zoom, press `Tab` from the repo heading to cycle through each tab link sequentially.
- **Keyboard shortcut:** Press `G` then `I` to jump directly to Issues, or `G` then `P` for Pull requests. These two-key shortcuts work from any page in the repository.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users (NVDA / JAWS)</summary>

1. Press `D` to jump to the **"Repository navigation"** landmark
2. Press `K` or `Tab` to navigate between the tab links

</details>

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users (VoiceOver)</summary>

1. `VO+U` → Landmarks rotor → navigate to **"Repository navigation"**

## The Files Table

> **See also:** [Appendix B: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md) lists the keyboard shortcuts for navigating repository file trees.

The files table is the core of the Code tab - it shows every file and folder in the repo.

### Reaching the files table

<details>
<summary>Visual / mouse users</summary>

The file table is the main panel of the Code tab, showing folders and files with their most recent commit message and how long ago each was changed. It’s visible immediately below the branch selector. Click any folder name to open it, or click a file name to view the file.

</details>

<details><summary>Low vision users (zoom, high contrast)</summary>

The file table occupies the main content area of the Code tab. At high magnification:

- The table has three columns: Name, Message (last commit), and Date. At 200%+ zoom, the Message and Date columns may be truncated. Hover over truncated text to see the full message in a tooltip.
- Folder icons appear before folder names; file icons appear before file names. In Windows High Contrast mode, these icons use system colors with visible outlines.
- Click any folder or file name to navigate into it. The names are standard links with hover underlines.
- Use `Ctrl+F` (browser Find) to search for a specific file name rather than scrolling a long file list at high zoom.

</details>

<details><summary>Screen reader users</summary>

Press `T` to jump to the next table on the page. The first table you will hit is usually the files table. NVDA will announce: “Table with [N] rows and 3 columns.”

</details>

The three columns are:

1. **Name** - file or folder name
2. **Message** - the most recent commit message that changed this file
3. **Age** - how long ago that commit happened

## Fork vs. Clone vs. Branch - What Is the Difference?

These three concepts are related but serve different purposes. Students often confuse them, so here is a side-by-side comparison.

The following table compares forks, clones, and branches across six dimensions.

| Dimension | Fork | Clone | Branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **What it creates** | A new repository on GitHub under your account | A local copy of a repository on your computer | A named pointer to a line of commits within the same repository |
| **Where it lives** | On GitHub (your account) | On your local machine | Inside any repository (local or remote) |
| **Relationship to original** | Linked (GitHub tracks the "parent" repo) | Independent copy (but has `origin` remote pointing to GitHub) | Part of the same repository |
| **When to use it** | Contributing to a repo where you do not have write access (most open source) | Working locally with Git and VS Code | Creating an isolated workspace for a feature, fix, or experiment |
| **How to contribute back** | Open a pull request from your fork to the original (upstream) repo | Push your branch to the remote, then open a PR | Open a pull request from your branch to `main` |
| **Workshop usage** | Not required for the Learning Room (you have direct write access) | Optional in Block 0 (for local Git work in Ch11+) | Required from Chapter 6 onward (feature branches for every PR) |

**In this workshop,** you will primarily use **branches** (Chapter 6 onward) and optionally **clone** the Learning Room for local work (Chapter 11). Forking is the standard workflow when contributing to repositories where you are not a collaborator, which is covered in [Contributing to Open Source](08-open-source-culture.md).

## GitHub Shortcuts for Repository Navigation - Spotlight

These are the GitHub built-in shortcuts you will use most on repository pages. They work by sending keystrokes directly to GitHub's JavaScript, so **enable Focus Mode first** (NVDA: `NVDA+Space`, JAWS: `Insert+Z`).

| Shortcut | What it does | When you need it |
| ---  | ---  | ---  |
| `?` | Show all shortcuts for this page | Any time - get the full context-specific list |
| `G C` | Jump to the Code tab | You're on Issues or PRs and want the file tree |
| `G I` | Jump to the Issues tab | You're browsing code and spot a bug to report |
| `G P` | Jump to the Pull Requests tab | You want to review open PRs |
| `G A` | Jump to Actions / workflow runs | You want to check CI status |
| `G G` | Jump to Discussions | You want to participate in project conversations |
| `G W` | Jump to Wiki | You want to view the repository wiki |

**How to use:** Press `G`, release it, then press the second letter. For example: press `G`, release, press `C` (not `G+C` together).
| `.` or `>` | Open repository in github.dev (VS Code in browser) | You want to edit a file or read code with VS Code shortcuts |
| `W` | Switch branch or tag | You want to browse a different branch of the code |
| `Y` | Expand URL to permanent canonical link | You want a link that always points to this exact commit |

**Press `?` now** on any GitHub repository page to see the live shortcut list for that specific context.

> **Screen reader tip - reading the shortcut dialog:** When the `?` dialog opens it is a modal overlay. Press `NVDA+Space` (NVDA) or ensure JAWS Virtual Cursor is active to browse the dialog content with `H` for headings and `↓` to read each shortcut. The dialog is **context-aware** - the shortcuts listed change based on the page you are on. Press `Escape` to close.

For the full shortcut system including issues, PRs, comments, and notifications, see [Screen Reader Cheat Sheet - GitHub Shortcuts section](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md#github-built-in-keyboard-shortcuts).

2. Activate the latest release link
3. Read the release notes (rendered Markdown with headings and lists)

### Scenario E: "I want to contribute - where do I start?"

1. Navigate to the Code tab
2. Look for `CONTRIBUTING.md` in the files table
3. Open it and read the contributing guidelines
4. Then go to Issues tab and filter by `good first issue`

## If You Get Stuck

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| Clone fails with "authentication required" | You need to sign in. See [Appendix D](appendix-d-git-authentication.md) for HTTPS authentication setup. |
| Cannot find the Code button for cloning | Press `B` to cycle buttons. The green "Code" button is above the file table. On narrow screens it may be hidden behind a "..." overflow menu. |
| File finder (`T` shortcut) does not open | Ensure you are in Focus Mode (NVDA: `NVDA+Space`). The `T` shortcut only works in the repository Code tab. |
| Forking creates a repo I did not expect | By default, forking copies only the default branch. Go to your fork's settings if you need to adjust. The original repo is untouched. |
| `G I` or `G P` shortcuts do not work | These require two separate key presses (G, release, then I or P), not simultaneous. Ensure Focus Mode is active first. |
| Everything else | Post a comment on your challenge issue describing what you tried. A facilitator or buddy will help. |

## Try It: The Five-Tab Tour

**Time:** 3 minutes | **What you need:** Browser with screen reader, signed in to GitHub

Navigate to the [Accessibility Agents repository](https://github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents) and do this:

1. **Code tab** - Press `D` to the "Repository navigation" landmark, then `K` to find "Code". Press `Enter`. You're on the file list.
2. **Issues tab** - Press `G` then `I` (Focus Mode first: `NVDA+Space`). How many open issues are there? Press `3` to jump through issue titles.
3. **Pull Requests tab** - Press `G` then `P`. Are there any open PRs?
4. **Find a file** - Press `T` (in Focus Mode) to open the file finder. Type `README` and press `Enter`. You just navigated straight to a file without scrolling.
5. **Read the README** - Press `1` to find the page title, then `2` to scan sections.

**You're done.** You just toured a real repository using only your keyboard.

> **What success feels like:** You visited four tabs and opened a file without touching a mouse. Every repository on GitHub has this same layout - you now know how to navigate all of them.

> ### Day 2 Amplifier - Accessibility Agents: `@daily-briefing`
>
> **Navigate every folder of [accessibility-agents](https://github.com/Community-Access/accessibility-agents) manually today before using any agent.** Find `.github/agents/`, open a `.agent.md` file, and read it - that file is how an agent knows what to do. You must understand the structure before you can evaluate whether an agent understood it correctly.
>
> Once you have mastered manual repository navigation:
>
> - **In VS Code** - `@daily-briefing morning briefing` sweeps every repository you have access to and delivers one prioritized document: open issues, PR status, CI results, security alerts, community reactions - all without opening a browser tab
> - **In your repo** - Fork [accessibility-agents](https://github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents) and the `.github/agents/` folder travels with every clone; every collaborator on your fork has access to the same agents you do
> - **In the cloud** - GitHub Agentic Workflows can generate daily status reports on a schedule, running inside GitHub Actions and posting digests to a designated issue thread - no VS Code, no local setup required
>
> *An agent's output only makes sense when you already know what it is describing. You are building that knowledge right now.*

> **Next Step:** Move on to [Chapter 04: The Learning Room](04-the-learning-room.md) to understand where we'll be practicing our new skills.

voiceRules.voiceExemplar:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
